title: Hearing Aids Market Size, Share & Forecast 2026-2032

market_overview.summary: This is the best-instrumented market in this batch and the one where a single unstated scope decision does the most damage. EHIMA's member companies sold 23.16 million hearing aids globally in 2025. Divide the published market sizes by that count and you get $380 to $652 per hearing aid — a factory-gate price. HearingTracker's survey of more than 1,100 buyers puts the measured average transaction at $2,694 a pair, or $1,347 an aid, so consumer spend on those 23.16 million units is roughly $31 billion, about 3.5 times the published figure. Demant proves the two-tier structure from inside one company: its retail revenue of DKK 10,724 million in 2025 exceeded its wholesale hearing-aid revenue of DKK 9,841 million. Four manufacturers' disclosed revenue totals about $11,769 million, which is 1.34x the published market — and the excess reconciles exactly once retail is stripped out, landing back on the manufacturer tier. We publish that tier, Global Market Insights' September 2025 series: $9.37 billion in 2026 to $13.67 billion by 2032 at 6.5%. The caution is that unit growth has decelerated to 2.1%, measured consumer prices are down 42% since 2018, and the manufacturers' own 2025 growth was roughly 2 to 3%.
key_trends: Unit growth is decelerating sharply: EHIMA members sold 21.81 million aids in 2023 (+7.7%), 22.69 million in 2024 (+4.0%) and 23.16 million in 2025 (+2.1%)

Measured consumer prices have collapsed: HearingTracker's buyer survey puts the average at $2,694 a pair against $4,672 in 2018, a 42% fall, with over-the-counter pairs transacting at $502 against $3,432 for prescription private-pay

The FDA's over-the-counter rule is the mechanism: published 17 August 2022 and effective 17 October 2022, it created an OTC category for adults with perceived mild-to-moderate loss and repealed the prior conditions for sale, with legacy devices required to comply by 14 April 2023

Retail is where the money now is, and the manufacturers know it: Demant's Hearing Care clinic revenue rose 8% to DKK 10,724 million in 2025 while its external wholesale hearing-aid revenue fell 2% to DKK 9,841 million

Manufacturer growth is near zero at the top of the industry: WS Audiology posted 0% organic growth in FY2024/25 on reduced United States benefit coverage, Demant's wholesale fell 2%, and GN's Hearing division grew 5% organic after 10% and 13% in the two prior years

Portfolio reshaping is under way: Sonova is divesting Consumer Hearing, now reported as discontinued operations, and renamed its Hearing Instruments business Wholesale and its Audiological Care business Retail with the FY2025/26 results
market_overview.adoption_level: 23.16 million units a year against 1.5 billion people with some hearing loss

drivers: Demographic inevitability: the WHO figure Global Market Insights itself cites puts 1.5 billion people with some degree of hearing loss, against 23.16 million units sold a year

The FDA's over-the-counter category, effective 17 October 2022, which removed the professional gatekeeping requirement for adults with perceived mild-to-moderate loss and has put devices on retail shelves at $502 a pair

Retail vertical integration, which is where the margin now accrues: Demant's clinic revenue rose 8% in 2025 on acquisitions, and Sonova has renamed its dispensing arm Retail and reports it inside the same segment as Wholesale

Platform refresh cycles driving replacement rather than first fittings: GN's 5% organic growth in 2025 was attributed specifically to the ReSound Vivia platform, and Sonova's second-half Wholesale acceleration to 10.9% to Phonak Infinio
Rechargeability and connectivity as replacement triggers, which shorten the effective device life of an installed base that historically replaced every five to seven years

Reimbursement expansion in individual markets, which moves whole cohorts at once — and whose withdrawal does the same in reverse, as WS Audiology's citation of reduced United States benefit coverage shows
restraints: Unit growth has fallen from 7.7% to 2.1% in two years on EHIMA's own series, which is the clearest single indicator in the market and sits far below every published revenue CAGR
Measured consumer prices are down 42% since 2018, so revenue can fall while units rise — the arithmetic every forecast in this category ignores
The manufacturers' own growth was roughly 2 to 3% in 2025: Demant's external wholesale revenue down 2%, WS Audiology 0% organic, GN 5% organic
Reduced benefit coverage in the United States, named explicitly by WS Audiology as a cause of its flat year, which shows how exposed unit volumes are to payer policy rather than to demand
Intense competition at the manufacturer tier, which Demant itself cites alongside slower-than-normal market growth as a drag on profitability despite a 17.2% EBIT margin

Published market figures are manufacturer-tier revenue presented without that label, so almost every reader of this category is working with a number roughly 3.5x smaller than the consumer spending they think it describes
opportunities: The gap between 23.16 million units a year and 1.5 billion people with some hearing loss, which is the largest untapped population in any market in this corpus
Over-the-counter and self-fitting devices at $502 a pair, which address a price-sensitive cohort that prescription channels at $3,432 a pair never reached
Retail and audiological care services, the tier that already generates more revenue than wholesale inside Demant and that no published definition of this market counts
Asia Pacific, which Global Market Insights projects as the fastest-growing region at 7.8% a year, and where unit penetration is far below North American and European levels
Paediatric fitting, projected at 8.5% a year against 6.3% for adults on the same publisher's figures, where lifetime device revenue per patient is highest
Consolidation of independent dispensing networks, which is visibly how Demant grew Hearing Care revenue 8% in a year when its wholesale business shrank
challenges: Four manufacturers' disclosed revenue totals about $11,769 million against published 2025 markets of $8.8 billion, $9.08 billion and $10.35 billion — disclosed revenue exceeds three of the five published totals, and Starkey is not even in the sum
The published figures imply $380 to $652 per hearing aid against measured consumer transactions near $1,347 per aid, a factor of two to three and a half that no publisher labels

One publisher's own distribution split puts e-commerce at $3.2 billion in 2024, or 38.6% of its total, in an industry where Demant's own clinic revenue is DKK 10,724 million and Sonova and Amplifon run large clinic networks. That figure is not credible and we publish nothing from it

Two versions of one publisher's forecast circulate on secondary sites and contradict each other — $29.58 billion by 2032 at 10.1% against $34.76 billion at 11.7% — with neither traceable to the publisher
The same house revised its own CAGR from 5.6% to 6.5% between editions while unit growth decelerated from 7.7% to 2.1%, which indicates how little of a published rate is a measurement
Currency fragmentation makes the industry hard to aggregate: the four disclosing manufacturers report in Swiss francs, Danish kroner and euros, and none of them publishes a USD figure

Its CHF 3,605.9 million of FY2025/26 continuing-operations revenue converts to roughly $4,587 million at our own approximate rate, which is more than half of the entire published 2025 market on its own. No share is disclosed and we assign none; trade commentary putting it between 25% and 31% carries no method and is not usable.

regulatory_landscape: The FDA over-the-counter hearing aid final rule, 87 FR 50698, published 17 August 2022 and effective 17 October 2022, established an OTC category at 21 CFR part 800 for air-conduction hearing aids that do not require surgical implantation, intended for people aged 18 and over with perceived mild-to-moderate hearing impairment. It amended 21 CFR parts 800, 801, 808 and 874, repealed the prior conditions for sale, revised labelling requirements and updated the Federal preemption exemption process. Devices already legally offered for sale before the effective date, including those with 510(k) clearance, had to comply by 14 April 2023, 240 days after publication. GAO noted the rule did not carry the 60-day delay the Congressional Review Act requires.

Prescription hearing aids remain 510(k) devices under 21 CFR part 874 and are dispensed under state licensure regimes for audiologists and hearing aid dispensers. The OTC rule did not change that pathway; it created a parallel one, which is why the same manufacturers now sell into two channels with roughly a sevenfold price difference between them.

Self-fitting air-conduction hearing aids were authorised through a separate De Novo classification before the OTC rule and are now the technical basis of most OTC products: the device must allow the user to program it to their own hearing without a professional fitting, which is the specific capability the OTC category requires.

EU Medical Device Regulation 2017/745 governs hearing aids placed on the EU market, with notified-body conformity assessment and post-market surveillance. The EU has no equivalent of the United States OTC category, which is one reason European price and channel structures differ from American ones and why a global market figure blends two regulatory regimes.

Reimbursement rather than regulation sets volumes in most countries. National systems in Denmark, Germany, France, the United Kingdom and Japan fund hearing aids through public or statutory schemes with their own tendering and price controls; in the United States traditional Medicare does not cover hearing aids, and coverage comes through Medicare Advantage supplemental benefits and employer plans. WS Audiology attributed a flat FY2024/25 directly to reduced benefit coverage in the United States, which shows how exposed unit volumes are to payer policy.

EHIMA's unit statistics are the de facto register for this market, and they are a voluntary trade-association compilation of member sales rather than a regulatory filing. EHIMA does not publish what share of world units its members represent, so the 23.16 million figure for 2025 is a floor on global volume rather than a total.

research_methodology.data_validation: The headline is one publisher's own base advanced at its own rate, labelled as interpolation: Global Market Insights' $8.8 billion for 2025 becomes $9.37 billion for 2026 and $13.67 billion for 2032 at 6.5%. The internal check is that the implied rate between our endpoints is 6.50%, identical to the stated rate. GMI was chosen because it carries a stated publication date and the longest published history in the set — five dated annual values from 2021 to 2025 — because it is the only source in the set read directly from the publisher's own page rather than through a search summary or secondary site, and because its $8.8 billion is the figure our reconciliation of disclosed manufacturer revenue lands on almost exactly. Five grounding tests were run. First, price per unit: EHIMA member companies sold 23.16 million hearing aids globally in 2025, so the published totals work out at $380 per aid on GMI's figure, $447 on MarketsandMarkets' and $652 on the Fortune figure circulating on secondary sites. HearingTracker's survey of more than 1,100 buyers puts the measured average transaction at $2,694 per pair, or $1,347 per aid, so 23.16 million units at consumer prices is roughly $31.2 billion — about 3.5 times GMI's total. The published figures are therefore manufacturer-tier revenue, and no publisher in the set says so. Second, Demant proves the two tiers from inside one company: in 2025 its Hearing Care retail revenue of DKK 10,724 million exceeded its external wholesale hearing-aid revenue of DKK 9,841 million, and its own retail arm bought DKK 2,632 million of aids internally while selling DKK 10,724 million of hearing care. Third, summing disclosed revenue: Sonova CHF 3,605.9 million, Demant DKK 22,971 million, WS Audiology EUR 2,579 million and GN's Hearing division DKK 7,214 million total about $11,769 million at our own approximate conversions, which is 1.34 times GMI's $8.8 billion, 1.30 times Ken Research's $9.08 billion and 1.14 times MarketsandMarkets' $10.35 billion — with Starkey, privately held, not in the sum and Amplifon, a pure retailer, outside every published definition. Fourth, the reconciliation: stripping retail out where it is disclosed gives Demant's wholesale at about $1,430 million, GN at $1,048 million and WS Audiology at about $2,796 million, totalling $5,274 million, to which Sonova's Wholesale and Starkey must be added; at plausible magnitudes for those two the manufacturer tier totals roughly $8.1 to $8.8 billion, which is GMI's figure. So the published figures are approximately right for the tier they measure and roughly 3.5 times too small for the tier a reader assumes. Fifth, a coherence test on growth: EHIMA unit growth decelerated from 7.7% to 4.0% to 2.1% across 2023-2025, measured consumer prices fell 42% from 2018 to 2026, and the manufacturers' own 2025 growth was roughly 2 to 3% — Demant's external wholesale down 2%, WS Audiology 0% organic, GN 5% organic — against published CAGRs of 5.6% to 11.7%. These are scope and plausibility tests, not market estimates. All currency conversions are ours at approximate rates implied by the USD figures the sources' own coverage printed alongside the local-currency ones; HearingTracker's prices are dated 2026 against our 2025 price base and are a survey of self-selected buyers rather than an average selling price; EHIMA's series covers member companies only and is therefore a floor on world units, with no published figure for members' share of global volume; the Sonova Wholesale and Starkey magnitudes used in the fourth test are our own and are published nowhere, and they appear in the notes file only; and dividing company revenue into a published market total compares differently constructed numbers. Regional, country and channel splits are published as empty arrays or plain strings: the only source offering them presents no method, and its own e-commerce figure of $3.2 billion for 2024 — 38.6% of its total — is not credible in an industry where Demant's clinic revenue alone is DKK 10,724 million. No vendor market share is published because none is disclosed, and the trade commentary putting Sonova between 25% and 31% carries no method.

faqs.question: How large is the hearing aids market?
faqs.answer: We publish $9.37 billion for 2026, rising to $13.67 billion by 2032 at 6.5%, derived from Global Market Insights' published $8.8 billion for 2025 at its own rate. Published 2025 estimates run from $8.8 billion to $15.11 billion — a 1.72x spread. The critical qualification is which tier that figure measures. Divided by EHIMA's 23.16 million units sold in 2025 it is $380 per hearing aid, which is a factory-gate price, not a retail one. Consumer spend on the same units is roughly $31 billion.

faqs.question: Why is consumer spending on hearing aids three times the published market size?
faqs.answer: Because the published figures are manufacturer revenue and nobody labels them as such. EHIMA's members sold 23.16 million aids globally in 2025. HearingTracker's survey of more than 1,100 buyers puts the measured average transaction at $2,694 per pair, or $1,347 per aid. That is $31.2 billion of consumer spend against an $8.8 billion published market — a factor of 3.5. The gap is the dispensing tier: clinics, audiology services, fitting and follow-up, all of which the consumer pays for and none of which the published figures count.

faqs.question: Is there direct evidence for the two-tier structure?
faqs.answer: Yes, from inside one company. Demant publishes its wholesale and retail revenue in the same statement. In 2025 its Hearing Aids external revenue — wholesale to third parties — was DKK 9,841 million and fell 2%, while its Hearing Care retail clinic revenue was DKK 10,724 million and rose 8%. Retail is larger than wholesale inside the same group. Its own retail arm bought DKK 2,632 million of aids internally and generated DKK 10,724 million of hearing care revenue. A market definition that counts only the first transaction captures less than half the money.

faqs.question: Does disclosed manufacturer revenue exceed the published market?
faqs.answer: It exceeds three of the five published figures. Sonova's CHF 3,605.9 million, Demant's DKK 22,971 million, WS Audiology's EUR 2,579 million and GN's DKK 7,214 million total about $11,769 million at our own approximate conversions — 1.34 times Global Market Insights' $8.8 billion, 1.30 times Ken Research's $9.08 billion and 1.14 times MarketsandMarkets' $10.35 billion. Starkey, the fifth major manufacturer, is privately held and not in that sum. Crucially, the excess reconciles: Sonova's and Demant's group figures include retail dispensing, and once that is stripped out the manufacturer tier lands back at roughly $8 to $9 billion.

faqs.question: Is the market really growing at 6.5%?
faqs.answer: Not on the evidence of 2025. EHIMA unit growth decelerated from 7.7% in 2023 to 4.0% in 2024 to 2.1% in 2025. Measured consumer prices per pair have fallen 42% since 2018. And the manufacturers' own disclosed growth last year was roughly 2 to 3%: Demant's external wholesale revenue fell 2%, WS Audiology posted 0% organic growth and GN managed 5% organic after 10% and 13% in the two prior years. Published CAGRs of 5.6% to 11.7% are not supported by any of those three series, and the same publisher revised its own rate up from 5.6% to 6.5% between editions while the industry slowed.

faqs.question: What did the FDA's over-the-counter rule do?
faqs.answer: It created a second channel with roughly a sevenfold price difference. The final rule was published on 17 August 2022 at 87 FR 50698 and took effect on 17 October 2022, establishing an OTC category for air-conduction hearing aids for adults aged 18 and over with perceived mild-to-moderate hearing loss and repealing the prior conditions for sale; devices already on the market had to comply by 14 April 2023. In HearingTracker's survey, OTC pairs transact at $502 against $3,432 for a prescription private-pay pair. That is the mechanism behind the 42% fall in measured consumer prices since 2018 — and a price collapse of that size while units grow 2.1% is not a revenue tailwind.

faqs.question: Which company leads the hearing aid industry, and what share does it hold?
faqs.answer: Sonova is the largest group by disclosed revenue at CHF 3,605.9 million of FY2025/26 continuing-operations sales, followed by Demant at DKK 22,971 million, WS Audiology at EUR 2,579 million and GN's Hearing division at DKK 7,214 million, with Starkey privately held and disclosing nothing. No company discloses a market share and we assign none. Trade and forum commentary putting Sonova anywhere between 25% and 31% carries no method and no source in any filing, and the estimates contradict each other.

executive_summary: Hearing aids is the best-instrumented market in this batch, and that is what makes its central defect provable rather than arguable. An industry trade body publishes unit shipments, four of the five major manufacturers publish revenue, one of them publishes wholesale and retail separately in the same statement, and a large buyer survey publishes measured transaction prices. Put them together and the published market sizes are revealed as a single unstated scope decision. EHIMA's members sold 23.16 million hearing aids globally in 2025; divide the published totals by that count and you get $380 to $652 per aid, which is a factory-gate price. HearingTracker's survey of more than 1,100 buyers puts the measured average at $2,694 per pair, or $1,347 per aid, so consumer spend on those same units is roughly $31.2 billion — about 3.5 times the $8.8 billion headline. Demant proves the two tiers from inside one company: 2025 retail clinic revenue of DKK 10,724 million, up 8%, against external wholesale hearing-aid revenue of DKK 9,841 million, down 2%. Four manufacturers' disclosed revenue totals about $11,769 million, exceeding three of the five published figures, with Starkey absent and Amplifon outside every definition — and the excess reconciles exactly once retail is stripped out, landing the manufacturer tier back at roughly $8 to $9 billion. We publish that tier: $9.37 billion in 2026 to $13.67 billion by 2032 at 6.5%. The warning attached is that unit growth has fallen from 7.7% to 2.1% in two years, measured consumer prices are down 42% since 2018 following the FDA's October 2022 over-the-counter rule, and the manufacturers' own 2025 growth was 2 to 3%.

A manufacturer makes a device and sells it at a factory-gate price of a few hundred dollars; a dispenser fits it, tunes it, follows the patient up and charges a bundled price several times higher. The published market figures measure the first transaction. They are approximately right for it — our reconciliation of disclosed manufacturer revenue lands within a few hundred million dollars of Global Market Insights' $8.8 billion for 2025 — and they are roughly 3.5 times too small for the thing most readers assume a market size means. The proof is available because this industry publishes unusually well. EHIMA gives units: 23.16 million in 2025. HearingTracker's buyer survey gives measured prices: $2,694 per pair. And Demant, uniquely, reports both tiers in one statement and shows retail revenue exceeding wholesale revenue inside the same company. The structural consequence is that the four groups with manufacturing businesses are all buying their way down the chain — Demant grew retail revenue 8% in a year when its wholesale fell 2%, and Sonova has renamed its two businesses Wholesale and Retail — while a pure retailer like Amplifon operates entirely outside every published definition of the market. Underneath all of it sits the number that frames the opportunity and the failure together: 23.16 million units sold a year against the 1.5 billion people WHO counts with some degree of hearing loss.
forecast_analysis: Our 6.5% is Global Market Insights' own rate on its own base, and the series reproduces that rate exactly. Whether 6.5% is defensible for the manufacturer tier is the harder question, and the evidence says it sits at the optimistic end of what the disclosed record supports. Three independent series all point lower. EHIMA's unit shipments decelerated from 7.7% growth in 2023 to 4.0% in 2024 to 2.1% in 2025. HearingTracker's measured consumer price per pair fell 42% between 2018 and 2026, with over-the-counter devices transacting at $502 against $3,432 for a prescription private-pay pair — the direct consequence of the FDA rule effective 17 October 2022. And the manufacturers themselves grew roughly 2 to 3% in 2025: Demant's external wholesale revenue down 2%, WS Audiology 0% organic on reduced United States benefit coverage, GN 5% organic after 10% and 13% in the two prior years. Sonova is the exception, with Wholesale accelerating to 10.9% in local currencies in the second half of FY2025/26 on the Phonak Infinio platform, which shows that a strong product cycle can still move share within a flat market. There is a coherent route to 6.5% at the manufacturer tier: wholesale prices hold while retail margins absorb the consumer price compression, so factory-gate revenue grows faster than consumer spend. Demant's own split is exactly that pattern under strain. But that argument supports the bottom of the published range, not the 10.1% and 11.7% figures circulating on secondary sites. Readers should forecast units — which EHIMA publishes and which is decelerating — and apply their own view of wholesale price, rather than accepting any published revenue CAGR for a market whose volume growth has halved twice in two years.
reader_takeaways: Decide which tier you mean. The published $8.8 billion is manufacturer revenue at about $380 per aid. Consumer spend on the same 23.16 million units is roughly $31 billion at measured transaction prices. The gap is the dispensing channel and no publisher labels it.
Use the unit series, not the revenue series. EHIMA publishes global member unit sales, and they grew 7.7%, then 4.0%, then 2.1% across 2023-2025 — a deceleration no published revenue CAGR reflects.

Read Demant's two revenue lines together. Retail at DKK 10,724 million rising 8% against wholesale at DKK 9,841 million falling 2%, in the same company, in the same year, is the clearest single piece of evidence about where the money in this industry has moved.

Note that four manufacturers already disclose more revenue than three of the five published markets contain — and that Starkey is private and Amplifon manufactures nothing, so neither appears in any of them.

Treat the FDA over-the-counter rule as a price event, not a volume event. OTC pairs transact at $502 against $3,432 prescription, measured prices are down 42% since 2018, and units grew 2.1% last year. That combination does not produce a double-digit revenue CAGR.
